passages.t: ‘Why do You stand far off?’ and the man who says ‘God has forgotten’
passages.happening:
Psalm 10 opens with a cry. “Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?” (verse 1).

Then it paints a long picture of a powerful, cruel man. “In pride the wicked pursue the needy” (verse 2). “For the wicked man boasts in the cravings of his heart; he blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD” (verse 3). “In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God” (verse 4).

We overhear what he says to himself: “I will not be moved; from age to age I am free of distress” (verse 6). He lies in wait: “in ambush he slays the innocent; his eyes watch in stealth for the helpless” (verse 8). “He lies in wait like a lion in a thicket” and “catches the lowly in his net” (verse 9).

And the deepest thing he tells himself: “God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This psalm continues Psalm 9. The broken alphabet poem runs on, and Psalm 10 has no heading of its own. In the Greek Old Testament the two are one psalm. Psalm 9 ended in confidence that God does not forget the needy. Psalm 10 tests that confidence hard. Where is God, while this goes on?

‘Stand far off’ and ‘hide’ are honest words. The psalmist does not pretend God feels near. He says what it feels like, and says it to God.

The picture of the wicked man comes from village life. ‘The villages’ were small settlements without walls, easy to raid. The man is like a hunter or a lion. He waits in hiding for the weak. ‘The needy’, ‘the helpless’, ‘the lowly’ are the poor, people with no one powerful to protect them.

Three times we hear, ‘He says to himself’ (verses 6, 11 and 13). The psalm lets us listen to his inner voice. ‘In all his schemes there is no God’ (verse 4) does not describe a thinker who has weighed the arguments and decided God does not exist. It describes a man who lives as if God does not matter. He does not say God is unreal. He says God has forgotten, God does not see, God will not call him to account. This is godlessness in practice: living as though no one will ever judge.

‘Trouble and malice are under his tongue’ (verse 7) pictures evil kept in his mouth, ready to use, like food held back to chew later.
passages.later:
Paul draws on verse 7 in his list of what sin does to every human mouth: “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness” (Romans 3:14).

The prophets name the same practical godlessness. Zephaniah speaks of men “who say to themselves, ‘The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad’” (Zephaniah 1:12). Jeremiah says the people “have lied about the LORD and said: ‘He will not do anything’” (Jeremiah 5:12).

Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, ‘Take it easy,’ and of God's answer: “You fool! This very night your life will be required of you” (Luke 12:20).

Hebrews answers the wicked man's claim that God never sees: “Nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight” (Hebrews 4:13).
passages.hard:
‘In all his schemes there is no God.’ Is this psalm about atheists?

No. The man in Psalm 10 is not someone who has thought hard about God and concluded he does not exist. This man's ‘no God’ is a way of living: he acts as if God will never notice and never judge, so that he can prey on the weak. Many readers call it practical atheism. A person can say all the right things about God and still live this way.

People today who do not believe in God, and who are honest about it, are not the target of this psalm. Many of them care deeply for the poor and the weak. The psalm's target is cruelty that tells itself no one is watching. That temptation lives in believers too.

There is a second hard thing here: the psalm's first question. Why does God seem far away when the poor are being hunted? The psalm does not answer with a theory. It brings the question to God, and then, in the second half, it asks God to act. The Bible lets that question be asked out loud.
passages.asks:
Listen to the voice that says, ‘God has forgotten; He never sees.’ Ask where you have let it speak in your own choices: in what you say when no one is checking, or how you treat people who cannot answer back.

And if you are the one who feels God is far off while you are hurt, the psalm gives you its first words to pray: ‘Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?’

passages.t: ‘Arise, O LORD’: the helper of the fatherless
passages.happening:
Now the psalm turns to God with a command. “Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God! Do not forget the helpless” (verse 12).

It answers the wicked man's lies one by one. He said God would never call him to account (verse 13). But, the psalm says to God, “You have regarded trouble and grief; You see to repay it by Your hand. The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless” (verse 14).

“Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found” (verse 15).

Then the psalm ends in confident praise. “The LORD is King forever and ever” (verse 16). “You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts” (verse 17). God will act “to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
‘Arise’ and ‘lift up Your hand’ are calls for God to act, as a king or a warrior rises to defend his people.

The word ‘forget’ ties the two psalms together. The nations forget God (9:17). The wicked man says God has forgotten (10:11). The psalmist asks God not to forget the helpless (10:12).

Verse 14 answers verse 11 directly. The wicked man said God ‘never sees’. The psalm says to God: You have seen. You have ‘regarded’, that is, looked carefully at, trouble and grief.

‘The fatherless’ in Israel were children whose father had died. In that world a father protected his household, held its land and spoke for it at the city gate. Without him a family could be robbed with little defence. Israel's law named God himself as their defender (Exodus 22:22-23; Deuteronomy 10:18). Verse 14 says the same of God: ‘You are the helper of the fatherless.’ It is a claim about who God is.

‘Break the arm’ means break the power of the wicked. The arm was a picture of strength. Like Psalm 3's ‘break the teeth’, it asks God to stop the violent from doing harm.

‘The men of the earth’ in verse 18 are mortal humans who use terror. The psalm ends with God as King and such people unable to frighten anyone any more.
passages.later:
Israel's law: “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:22-23). God “executes justice for the fatherless and widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18). Another psalm calls him “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5).

James says that true religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).

The ending, ‘The LORD is King forever and ever’, rings out again in Revelation: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).
passages.asks:
The psalm calls God ‘the helper of the fatherless’ and asks him to act for them. James says that those who follow him will do the same. Ask who in your church or your street has lost the one who stood up for them, and how you might stand with them.

When you see cruelty go unpunished, pray verse 12: ‘Arise, O LORD. Do not forget the helpless.’ Then let the last verse shape your hope: the LORD is King, and terror will not have the last word.
